content.content:
=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at

# Conversions and overloading: the judgement

## For Pavol

### Where you are

- On the fork of question A you chose option 2, "the generic arm, at `ZZ64`", on the condition that it is sound. Then you asked for the wider picture: one rule, not "rule on the rule", and your own idea weighed beside the others.
- The soundness check is in: option 2 is sound in the form answer 9 already gives it. The nine steps are in: twelve ways, the peers, the history, and your idea written in a sound form (the note's way 4).
- This judgement takes it from there. It measures nothing; every number is on record.

### The terms, as this note uses them

- A **declaration** (an "arm") is one definition of a name. `op(a: Any, b: Any)` is one; `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` is another.
- A call **fits** a declaration when each argument's type is the parameter's type or below it. Among the declarations a call fits, the **most specific** runs: the one with the narrowest parameter types.
- A **conversion** (the specification's word is coercion) is declared by the type it goes into: `ZZ64` declares `coerce(x: ZZ32)`. Since your answer 8 only exact conversions are automatic: a narrower integer into a wider one, and `ZZ32` or a numeral into `RR64`.
- A **generic** declaration has a type parameter with a **bound**. Read as the type group's 2011 model reads it, which is your answer 9: it fits a call when some type within the bound fits. `op[\T extends Number\]` fits a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` as they are, with `T = Number`.
- A **self-naming bound** is `T extends Integral[\T\]`: `T` must be a type that implements `Integral` at itself, so `T` is one integer type, never "some number". A `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` fit such a generic only after one is converted. It is the library's usual bound.
- A **plain** declaration has no type parameter. A **catch-all** is a plain declaration over a wide type, `Any` or `Number`, that fits nearly everything.
- An **instance** of a generic is the generic at one type, `op` at `ZZ64`. On the compiled path each instance is a class stamped at load time from the generic's template.
- **Promotion** is your answer 8: a generic call over mixed widths takes the narrowest type every argument converts into, `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, and converts the narrower argument.

### The two rules that met on your fork

- The designers' rule, in the coercion chapter: if any declaration fits without conversion, choose among those; convert only when nothing fits. The checker's team code has ranked this way since 2009. Walk has since rung C.
- Your answer 8: inside a generic call, convert to the narrowest type rather than keep the common parent type unconverted.
- Your fork: `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, called with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`. The generic at `ZZ64` needs one conversion. The catch-all needs none.
- Batch N's two shadows ran the catch-all there (the note's way 1). That reading is out. It decides what fits by the instance the promotion picks, so a declaration can fit a wide static type and not fit a narrower one, and the run-time choice can be less specific than the static one. That breaks the specification's promise and splits the two paths (measured, `O2Wide`).

### The one rule, and why there is no contradiction

- The rule: **a conversion is applied to make a call possible; it never changes which body runs when a body already fits.**
- Answer 8 obeys it. Choosing `ZZ64` over `Number` inside one generic does not change which body runs. It is the same body, stamped at a narrower type. So the designers' order and your answer 8 are one rule at two levels: first the declaration (the body), by the designers' order; then the instance (the type the body is stamped at), by promotion.
- On your fork: does the generic fit as it is? Yes, on its declared types, with `T = Number`. It is more specific than the catch-all, so it is chosen. Then promotion stamps it at `ZZ64` and converts the `ZZ32`. That is your option 2, in the form the soundness check found sound ("reading A", the note's way 2).
- What it does not reach: a generic with a self-naming bound beside a catch-all. Such a generic does not fit mixed widths as they are, so the catch-all, which does, runs. The library has no such pair, and neither does microGPT; measured, nothing in the tests, demos or microGPT reaches the fork at all. With no catch-all beside it, a self-bound generic is promoted and converted like any other (measured, `O2FbLone`).

### Your idea, and what it becomes

- Your words: "if there is a conversion to a specific type, it should be applied. And only if all combinations are exhausted and we haven't reached a specific implementation, then we go to a plain implementation."
- Its sound form is the note's way 4: list every declaration and every instance that fits, with or without conversions; if one is more specific than all the others by the coercion chapter's own relation, run it, converting what it needs; otherwise fall back to the designers' order. It is C#'s rule.
- It gets three things right. It treats generic and plain arms alike. It makes answer 8 a special case. It reaches the self-bound generics.
- I recommend against it, for five reasons.
  - It treats a conversion as free. On the JVM a conversion is work: a new `ZZ64` object made from a `ZZ32`, a big-number rational made from an integer. Way 4 adds a conversion to every call where a converted arm outranks an arm that fits as it is. The designers' order never converts when an arm fits.
  - Most specific is not fastest. Under way 4, `z1 =/= z2` for two `ZZ32`s runs `QQ`'s `=/=`, converting both to rationals, because `QQ` is below `Any`. It stays so until a library line removes `QQ`'s redundant `=/=`. Every such shape in every future library file is a trap of the same kind.
  - The speed you want comes from the library, and the team's own compiled library shows how. It declares no `=` over `Any` or `Number`; each number type declares its own, and equality of other objects comes from `Equality[\T\] comprises T`. Under the designers' order, `z = 0` then reaches `ZZ32`'s own `=` with the numeral converted, because no catch-all fits first. Your idea at the library level is exactly that discipline: a specific arm at every type, no catch-all that fits first. At the language level it is C#'s order, and only C#'s.
  - The designers are unanimous. Their specification, their checker (Hilburn, 2009) and their compiled library all follow the designers' order; their later model (2011, 2012) is silent on conversion. Java, C++, Swift and Julia run an arm that needs no conversion before one that does; only C# ranks by the conversion's target. Your words of 09-23: "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
  - Its price. It reverses the designers' sentence for plain arms too: `f(ZZ64)` beats `f(Any)` for a `ZZ32`. Two gated tests and one planned assertion are restated. A call that runs today, rung Q's `ee(5)`, becomes a refusal. The proof appendix is rescoped. Walk needs a further condition to stay sound where a variable's declared type is wider than its value. The code generator's defect for two competing generic arms must be fixed first. And a probe of both paths comes before any batch.

### What your principle of speed buys on today's compiled path

- The generic at `ZZ64` is a stamped class called with no run-time test: a static load, one conversion, one call. The catch-all is reached through a dispatcher that looks up the arguments' types and tests them, two lookups and up to three tests, then the call. The JIT sees one type at the stamped call site and can inline it.
- Nothing is unboxed either way. The stamped class renames the type; it does not change the representation. The values stay `FZZ64` objects. That is phase 6's work, your storage decision of 09-19.
- The two arms run two different bodies the programmer wrote. Choosing an arm is not choosing between two compilations of one body.
- No timing was taken; none would decide between the ways. Interpreter speed decides nothing, by your rule of 09-19.

### Decision 1. Which order governs when conversions meet overloading

**The question.** When a generic arm fits a call as it is on its declared types but needs a conversion once promoted, and another arm fits as it is, which runs, and by what rule written into the specification?

**Context.**
- The specification's order (convert only when nothing fits) is explicit for plain arms and silent on generics with promotion. Answer 9 already reads applicability and specificity on declared types.
- Measured: today both paths run the generic unconverted; batch N's shadows run the catch-all; your fork's generic at `ZZ64` runs and dispatches correctly when written out (`O2Explicit`, `O2Z64`).
- The library and microGPT reach no such pair. The checker lacks the ambiguity check the specification assumes, whichever way is chosen.

**Options.**
1. **The designers' order on declared types, then promotion** (the note's way 2; your option 2 as answer 9 reads it). Your fork runs the generic at `ZZ64`. A catch-all that fits as it is still wins over a self-bound generic. Plain arms are unchanged. Touches: rung I ranks a promoted candidate on its declared types and does not count the promotion's conversion; rung K re-instantiates the chosen generic after the choice (one edit its brief reserved, now permitted); rung T states the rule at two levels; one cross-reference sentence in the coercion chapter, in batch 7b's specification rung. Costs: the library keeps the discipline the team's compiled library has, a specific arm at each type and no catch-all that fits first in a fast family; rung Q meets that at `=`.
2. **Most specific wins by the coercion chapter's relation, converting to reach it; the designers' order only as the tie-breaker** (way 4, your idea in sound form, C#'s rule). Your fork the same; self-bound generics reached; plain arms reversed too. Touches: the coercion chapter's resolution section rewritten with the original kept; rung I ranks over both attempts; rung K computes converted candidates on every overloaded call; rung W; the proof appendix; two tests; one assertion; `QQ`'s `=/=`; the two-generic code-generator defect; a probe. Costs: a conversion added per call where a converted arm outranks an unconverted one; batch N delayed by the probe and by phase 5's defect pulled forward; walk needs a condition to stay sound.
3. **Today's answer: the promotion is skipped when another arm fits** (way 7). Your fork runs the generic unconverted at the common parent type. Costs: an exception to answer 8 in rungs I, K and T; whether a call converts depends on an unrelated arm.

**A yes to 1** commits you to batch N as briefed with the three amendments, the coercion chapter's sentence in 7b, and the library discipline above. **A no** (option 2) costs the list under option 2 and reverses the designers' sentence for plain arms.

**Recommendation.** Option 1: the designers' order on declared types, then answer 8's promotion, one rule at two levels.

### Decision 2. Row 484: `b MAX 1` for a `ZZ64` `b`

**The question.** What makes `b MAX 1` answer under walk for a `ZZ64` `b`, as `b + 1` does?

**Context.**
- The candidates are `QQ`'s `MAX` and the `MAX` that `ZZ64` inherits from the generic order traits, whose `self` is typed as the trait. Neither is more specific than the other by the chapter's relation, so walk stops, "Ambiguous coercion"; the checker takes whichever comes first. Decision 1 leaves this as it is: no ordering rule settles it.
- `ZZ64` declares its own `+` and `<=`, which is why `b + 1` answers. `QQ`, `RR64`, the compiler library and the specification's `ZZ` declare their own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`.
- After the numeral switch (rung Q), `ZZ32`'s `b MAX 1` and the library's own `0 MAX (index - 1)` meet the same tie, by reading.

**Options.**
1. **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`**: 15 declarations, about 30 short library lines and one test; no model line; the checker count reported. Every such call then answers at answer 8's type.
2. **Walk reads an inherited method's `self` as the receiver's type.** Code on both paths and a revision against the specification's sentence on `self`; `QQ`'s still ties with the one left.
3. **Leave it.** Programs write `widen(1)`; `ZZ64` and `ZZ` stop; rung Q meets the library's own sites.

**A yes to 1** commits you to a small library rung in batch N's first run, before rung Q. **A no** leaves row 484 open and rung Q to meet it.

**Recommendation.** Option 1, the library's own device.

### Taken as defaults, listed for your review

Each follows the record's standing reading: a default that reverses nothing of yours is taken and listed. One word from you changes any of them.
- **Walk promotes from run-time types.** Walk has no static types. Where a variable is declared wider than its value (`n: Number` holding a `ZZ32`), the compiled path runs the generic at `Number` and walk at `ZZ64`: the same body, a narrower instance, the value inside the declared type. It does not reach a program whose declared types are concrete, as microGPT's are. A ledger row records it.
- **Q1's default is stated once**, in the inference chapter, as the tie rule for a numeral alone: when a numeral's candidate types are incomparable, it is read as `ZZ32` (`ZZ64` or `ZZ` by magnitude), whether an instance or a converted declaration is being chosen. It reaches nothing but numerals.
- **Batch N launches next, when 7C lands, with the three amendments; no probe first.** Probe K and the checker shadow already measured the rule over the tests, demos, microGPT and the library; the one shape this judgement changes is reached by no recorded call.
- **Three findings that stand under every way.** `exactValue` has no case for a numeral, so after the switch `x = 0` would answer wrongly through `Number`'s `=`: a requirement of rung Q, with a ledger row for that shape's cost. The stock compiled crash on a promoted generic beside `op(ZZ64, ZZ64)`: a ledger row, closed by rung I's test. The code generator's defect for two competing generic arms: it stays on phase 5's list as answer 9 placed it; decision 1 gives it no new reach.

----- 2026-09-28T20:08:52.590Z 2897
Both judgements are in, both for batch 7b. Here is item 26; item 30 comes after you answer.

**Question:** four passages of the specification still read a `comprises` clause at the level of types, and since batch 7C that no longer holds. Restate them at the level of values, narrow 7C's rule so they hold again, or leave them?

**Refresher.**
- `trait S comprises { U, V }` closes `S`, and there are two ways to read it.
- The type reading: every type under `S` is under `U` or `V`, like Java's `sealed`.
- The value reading: every value of `S` is a value of `U` or `V`. A trait in between adds no values but is still a type.
- Batch 7C took the value reading on your option 1. That is what lets `Integral` stand between `AnyIntegral` and the five integer types.

**Context.**
- Two passages, the intersection example and the Meet Rule's example, draw a type conclusion from two clauses. It holds for values, not for types. The other two say "every immediate subtype", which can now differ from the listed types.
- Measured: three programs the text allows break the type statement. The checker refuses them and walk runs them. One of those shapes has been accepted since 2009, so the break predates 7C.
- The designers' 2012 texts read a clause as values wherever they use one. Their 2009 future-work list names the fix for the Meet Rule: "the coverage check".
- Both implementations already read values wherever they use a clause. The one exception is finding a meet, row 492, where both refuse the specification's own example.
- Batch 7b's specification rung is about to rewrite the chapter that holds the Meet Rule.

**Options.**
1. Restate the four passages at the level of values, define "covers" once, add the closed-trait case to the Meet Rule, and repair row 492 on both paths, all in batch 7b.
   - Touches: four specification files and the proof appendix, plus tens of lines each in the checker and in walk.
   - Costs: no new rung, but three rungs grow. Two expected-failure tests become passing tests, and three or four tests are added. No library or model line changes.
2. Narrow 7C's rule so the type statements hold.
   - It is a rule of ours with no source in the designers' texts, and it refuses a shape accepted since 2009.
   - Row 492 still needs the same checker and walk work, and two of the passages still need option 1's text.
3. Leave them. It costs nothing now, but a false sentence stays, and the same text and code come back later as a second rewrite of that chapter.

**A

You're close. Three corrections, then why `Any` isn't just the status quo.

**`Any` and `Bottom` are opposite ends.**
- `Any` is the top: every type sits below it, and every value in Fortress belongs to it.
- `Bottom` is the bottom: it sits below every type and has no values at all. It's the type of an expression that never returns a value, such as `throw`.
- The question in item 3 is only about the top. When a generic declaration writes `[\T\]` with no bound, what may `T` be?

**What `Object` is in Fortress.** It isn't Scala's `object` keyword, although Fortress has a similar keyword:
- A Fortress `object` declaration makes values. Without parameters it's a singleton, like Scala's `object`. With parameters, like `object Just[\T\](x: T)`, it's a constructor, much like a Scala case class. So your memory connects the right things.

20:- F-26 **Walk chooses between a generic declaration and another on their declared domains, not by the order they are written in.** It builds P-45 under walk. A generic trait's functional method is still compared by its instances; a generic dotted method is compared on its declared domain where exactly one of the two declared domains lies inside the other (`MethodStaticArgDeclaredDomain`). A generic instance chosen by converting an argument dispatches again, except for overloaded methods. The symbolic instance reads the static parameters' kinds and bounds, not a `where` clause. Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 5.1.
152:- F-137 **Under `walk`, a generic call's static arguments are inferred with coercion, by P-74's promotion, also for the declaration that an overloaded call chooses (P-46).** A lone type parameter takes the narrowest of its arguments' run-time types, their coercion targets and its bounds that admits every argument. So `ZZ32` with `ZZ64` gives `ZZ64`, and `ZZ64` with `RR64` gives the declared bound. With no narrowest candidate, the parameter takes its bound (F-141). Where a static type is wider than its value, the two paths instantiate differently (row 509). Not reached: rows 432, 486, 510 and 511, and a numeral alone at a bound it does not meet (P-76). Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 9.
171:- F-252 **Under walk, two functions with static parameters that no pair of parameter types excludes are read on their declared domains, each over its own instances, by the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, and a pair whose declared domains are equal is refused even where the parameter check orders it.** Walk's parameter-by-parameter check passes a pair it finds excluding; a pair of two own generics it refuses is read by `genericPairValid` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:766`), whether or not an exclusion was withdrawn; a pair it passes by order, one at least an own generic and the other an own generic or plain, whose declared domains each lie inside the other is refused, "fails because their parameter lists have the same types" (`:533-540`, `sameDeclaredDomains` `:806`), since the check reads a type parameter as strictly below its bound. Limits: the Meet Rule's search matches the two domains only where their parameter types are, position by position, instances of one generic type or static parameters (row 539), beside which a pair whose parameter types exclude only together is read over its whole parameter type where neither has a `where` clause of its own (F-258; row 787); instances of one generic type at different ground arguments do not exclude in the check (row 416); a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on the instance a call makes, and so is a generic dotted method except where exactly one of the two declared domains lies inside the other (F-253). Gated by `tests/DispatchRenamedGenericArmWalk`, `DispatchSwappedGenericArmWalk`, `GenericPairNestedBoundsWalk` (load and dispatch), `GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`, `GenericBesidePlainSameDomain` (refused), `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-generic-pairs/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5. The Return Type Rule, where one of two own generics lies inside the other, is read at the instance of the outer one that holds the inner one's declared domain only where that instance stands for every instance applicable to an argument of the inner one (`returnRuleAtEveryInstance`, `OverloadedFunction.java` at 36afa7eb1): each static paramete
172:- F-253 **Under walk, a dotted call that writes no static argument infers a generic method's own static arguments, and the method is chosen on its declared domain.** Walk takes the instance from the arguments' run-time types, as at a call of a generic function, whether the method is alone under its name or among its receiver's overloads. Against another method of the set it is compared on its declared domain where exactly one of the two declared domains lies inside the other, as an own generic is. A method that a trait declares reads its bounds, and the types into which its arguments convert, in the trait's method environment, where its instances evaluate their types (`GenericMethod.getTypeEnv`, `interpreter/evaluator/values/GenericMethod.java:106`, read at `EvaluatorBase.java:491`, `:567`, `:646` and `:651` at 5c5dee93d). So it takes the instance that the same method declared in an object takes: a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` give `Box[\ZZ64\]` with the `ZZ32` converted, and a bounded type parameter that nothing fixes takes its bound. An inherited generic functional method beside an object's plain one is chosen where only it applies. A call that the inference with coercion does not instantiate, as one whose argument lies outside a bound, still fails with an error of unification that reads no bound ('Cannot unify Int ... with Shape ... abm=K=(Int,Any)'), where the same method declared in an object fails with another error ('Meet(Int, Shape) not a singleton'): the unification keeps the team's read (`EvaluatorBase.java:886` at 5c5dee93d). Rung L's generic `distribute` then runs the nested reductions under walk (F-248). Gated by `tests/MethodStaticArgInference.fss`, `MethodStaticArgOverloadedReceiver.fss`, `MethodStaticArgDeclaredDomain.fss`, `NestedReductionFusion.fss`, `TraitGenericMethodInference.fss` and `InheritedGenericFunctionalMethodBesidePlain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-method-sargs/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 2; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-trait-method-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 4, and its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3.
203:- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule the compiled checker builds.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred. A lone type parameter takes the narrowest of its arguments' types and their coercion targets, else its bound; one that nothing fixes takes its bound, never `BottomType`. The checker departs only at `ZZ32` with `NN32` on the compiler prelude (row 442). Callouts give walk's departures (rows 587, 589, 591, 592, 616). Plain tests gate the lone parameter on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md` section 3.1.

component DispatchConvertedAgain
export Executable

(* A call that converts an argument for the generic declaration dispatches again, on the converted values, to the plain declaration they fit. *)

opz[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): String = "generic[" kindOf(a) "," kindOf(b) "]"
opz(a: ZZ64, b: ZZ64): String = "plain64[" kindOf(a) "," kindOf(b) "]"

kindOf(x: Any): String = typecase x of
    ZZ32 => "ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => "ZZ64"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
    z: ZZ32 = 3
    w: ZZ64 = widen(4)
    assert(opz(z, w), "plain64[ZZ64,ZZ64]", "the generic declaration takes a ZZ32 and a ZZ64 at ZZ64 by converting the ZZ32; the converted call then fits the plain declaration on ZZ64, the more specific, and runs it")
    assert(opz(w, w), "plain64[ZZ64,ZZ64]", "two ZZ64 values take the plain declaration, whose domain lies inside the generic declaration's")
    assert(opz(z, z), "generic[ZZ32,ZZ32]", "two ZZ32 values take the generic declaration at ZZ32, the only one that fits them")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

No, I don't think you made a mistake. The two choices fit together, and here's why.

**What the JVM does:** array lengths and indices are Java `int`, a signed 32-bit number, which is `ZZ32`. Java has no unsigned integers, so there is no JVM type for a count that can't be negative. Instead, the JVM refuses a negative length or index at run time with an exception. The longest array is 2^31 − 1, about 2G elements.

**What you decided:**
- **Ranges are `ZZ32`** (27 Sept, "that's the largest array size on JVM"). This matches the JVM's `int`. Ranges must be signed anyway, because a loop like `-5:5` counts through negative numbers.
- **A size is an `NN32`** (also 27 Sept, following the specification). `NN` means natural numbers, 0 and up; `ZZ` means all integers, negative too. A size can't be negative, so `NN32` states that in the type. The same decision says the array design refuses a length over 2^31 − 1 where it makes storage, which is exactly the JVM's limit.

**So the two numbers are not supposed to be the same type.** A size says "how many", which is never negative. An index or range bound says "where", which can be negative in loops, and Fortress arrays can even start at a nonzero base index. They meet only where a size is used as a bound, as in `0#n`.

That meeting point is exactly the question on the table. Option 1 says a size converts to `ZZ32` there, the way a numeral does. It always fits, because the array design already refuses sizes over 2^31 − 1 where storage is made. If a size larger than that were ever used as a number, the conversion would refuse it, just as it refuses an oversized numeral.

**Nine steps?** I don't think this needs one. The facts are few and settled: the JVM's `int`, the specification's `NN32`, the library's own `b0#s0`, and your two decisions. They agree with option 1. If you'd still like one for certainty, it's one Opus worker, about 0.5M tokens, and it would finish before batch N's slot opens (N waits for 6.5's first run anyway, about 2 hours).

**Ask:** option 1, or a nine-steps write-up first?

content.content:
## The judgement in full

For the coordinator and the planners of batches N and 7b. Each decision with its reasons and its citations. "Measured" cites a capture on record; "by reading" is mine.

### 1. The rule

**Decided: way 2**, reading A of `option-2-soundness.md`: the coercion chapter's order over declarations, with applicability and specificity taken on declared, quantified domains as answer 9 words them, and answer 8's promotion as the instantiation of the selected declaration, its coercions inserted statically and the rewritten call dispatching on the converted values.

**Stated for the specification** (rung T's inference chapter; batch 7b's rung S for the coercion chapter's cross-reference):

> *Resolution* (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:472-476`, `:533-553`, unchanged in substance). For a static call `f(A)` or `A₀.f(A)`, let Σ be the declarations of `f` applicable to the call without coercion, a declaration with static parameters being applicable when some instance within its bounds is (`Papers/Types/setup.tick:393-397`; answer 9), and compared on those quantified domains. If Σ is not empty, its most specific declaration is selected. Otherwise, among the declarations applicable with coercion, the one whose parameter type is no less specific (`⪯`, `:486-513`) than every other's is selected; the overloading rules guarantee that it exists and is unique, and where they do not, the call is a static error.
>
> *Instantiation* (the inference chapter). The static arguments of the selected declaration are then inferred: a static parameter takes the narrowest type, under `⪯`, that every argument constraining it is substitutable for (`:417-432`), its bounds permitting; for number arguments this is the narrowest type every one of them converts into (answer 8). The coercions this instance needs are inserted into the call statically, like any coercion resolved statically (`:584-591`).
>
> *Dispatch* (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The rewritten call dispatches at run time, by subtyping and without further coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.
>
> *Numerals* (Q1; decision 4 below). Where a numeral's candidate types are incomparable under `⪯`, in either step, the numeral is read as `ZZ32`, or as `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit.

**Reasons.**
- One principle at two levels, not two rules. A conversion makes a call possible and never changes which body runs when a body already fits (`conversions-coercions.tex:279-282`, `:472-476`). Answer 8 chooses among instances of one body; it never chooses between bodies. So the designers' order and answer 8 do not conflict once applicability is read on declared domains, which answer 9 already decided (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` section 3.4: "inference instantiates the chosen declaration; it does not precede the comparison").
- Sound, with one sentence. `option-2-soundness.md` section 1: the Meet Rule, the uniqueness facts and the appendix lemma speak of declared domains, which reading A does not change (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:247-274`, `:449-470`; `Specification/appendices/overloading-coercion.tex:75-96`). Section 2: the converted call's re-dispatch to `plain64` is type-safe by the return-type rule over every instance (measured, `O2Z64` on the rule and opt2 builds). Section 3: the Meet Rule does its job (`O2Meet`, every build). Section 4: it is answer 9's own order.
- The designers' record is unanimous for this order, and the type group's later word does not contradict it. The coercion chapter (2007-2009; `0f49d8698`). The checker's coercion-first ranking (Hilburn, 2009-08-18, `fc99e1ef2`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1085-1095`, opened and read). The compiled library, whose `=` and `=/=` are per type with no arm over `Any` or `Number` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:123-124`, `:167-168`, `:229-230`, `:299-300`, `:359-360`, `:412-413`, `:445`), general equality being `Equality[\T\] comprises T` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:24-26`), so that under this order `z = 0` reaches `ZZ32`'s own `=` with the numeral converted: by reading, Σ is empty, and `(ZZ32, ZZ32) ⪯ (ZZ64, ZZ64)` and `⪯ (ZZ, ZZ)` because `IntLiteral`, the one type that converts into `ZZ32`, excludes both (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`). The 2011 paper and Welterweight have no coercion (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`; `Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`, `:187-193`). Protocol principle 1 and POSITIONS 2026-09-23 give the later word more weight where the two conflict; here nothing conflicts.
- The peers. Java (strict invocation before loose), C++ (an exact match beats a promotion beats a conversion, and a user-defined conversion ranks lowest), Swift (a score that counts conversions first) and Julia (never converts in dispatch; the library's catch-alls promote) all put an unconverted arm first; C# alone ranks by the conversion's target (`conversion-overloading-ways.md` section 6). Pavol asked for the rule "from type theory and the peers' implementations"; the peers' majority is the designers' order.
- Speed. Under this order no call converts when an arm fits; a conversion is a run-time allocation (`option-2-soundness.md` section 6, `coerce_ZZ64(FZZ32)` per call). The fast path is the library's arm at the exact type, which the compiled library's design reaches on every call. On the fork itself the stamped instance is taken, with no dispatch test (`option-2-soundness/captures/javap-O2Explicit.txt`).
- What Pavol's idea becomes, and why it is not taken. Way 4 is its sound form (`conversion-overloading-ways.md` sections 8 and 9, way 4): "specific" read as the chapter's `⪯`, a candidate taken only when it is `⪯` every other, the designers' order as the fallback; unique by antisymmetry (`conversions-coercions.tex:503-509`). Not adopted because: (i) it ranks a conversion as free, adding one per call wherever a converted arm outranks an unconverted one; (ii) most specific is not fastest, `z1 =/= z2` reaching `QQ`'s `=/=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:71`, `:406`; by reading); (iii) it reverses `:472-476` for plain arms (`p(NarrowOf(1))` to `p(Wide)`, `ProjectFortress/tests/CoercionOverloadRungC.fss:45` and `compiler_tests/XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC.fss`; `ee(5)` refused by rung R's rule under answer 12); (iv) its walk half decides from run-time types and needs a further condition where a program's own conversion goes into a trait excluding the static type (the ways note, way 4's soundness paragraph); (v) it reaches shapes no library or microGPT declaration has (`before-n-questions.md` A.3; `PROBE-K.md:11`, `:17`), at the price of a probe, phase 5's defect 3 pulled forward (`O2Excl` under opt2), the proof appendix rescoped, and tens of lines in the checker and in walk's per-call dispatch, which caches nothing for an overloaded method. C# is one peer; the designers are unanimous. Way 4 is recorded here as the way back if a future library shape needs it, priced as above.
- The other ways. Way 1 (batch N as the shadows built it) is unsound: applicability is not closed downward, so the specification's promise that the run-time choice is at least as specific fails (`O2Wide`, `option-2-soundness.md` section 2; `advanced/overloading.tex:466-468`). Way 3 is unsound as it stands (`O2Tie`). Ways 5 and 6 add refusals or a second relation. Way 7 reverses part of answer 8. Way 8 refuses calls the specification promises an arm. Way 9 breaks mixed-type arms (`QQ`'s `^(self, other: ZZ64)`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:422`). Way 11 is unimplemented and deferred by answer 8. Way 12 is a code-generation design for phase 6, noted under what is left open. Way 10 composes with the decision and is its library half.

### 2. Reach into plain declarations

**Decided: not wanted.** It comes only with way 4. Under the decision plain arms follow `:472-476` as today: `p(NarrowOf(1))` prints `p(Any)` (`CoercionOverloadRungC.fss:45` stands; `XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC.fss` stays row 390's expected failure); rung Q's `ee(5)` takes the `Any` arm and prints 2 (`O2Pos`, every build; rung Q's test as planned); the integer `=/=` never reaches `QQ`; the two-generic dispatcher defect gains no reach, since `two(z, z)` runs the plain arm under reading A, neither generic's declared domain holding two `ZZ32`s (measured on the stock and rule builds, `O2Excl`); walk's remaining split is rung K's instance split alone (section 3).

### 3. Walk at run time

**Decided: walk chooses the declaration on the domains it compares today, the join instantiation, until rung W compares declared domains; it then re-instantiates the chosen generic by the promotion from the arguments' run-time types and converts at binding. It does not instantiate without conversion.**
- Why promote from run-time types. Walk has no static types, so "the checker's answer" is unknowable to it. Instantiating at the join without conversion, the later model's run-time instantiation (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:187-193`), would give up answer 8 under walk everywhere, including the silent 32-bit arithmetic on a `ZZ64` variable that answer 8 ends (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, answer 8, its last sentence). For a program whose static types are concrete, as microGPT's are, the two paths then agree on arm and instance.
- Where they differ. A variable declared wider than its value (`same(n, w)`: compiled `[ZZ32, ZZ64]`, walk `[ZZ64, ZZ64]`, `O2Lone`; `O2Wide`), and an argument typed `Any` (`O2Lone`, `op(a, aw)`). The same body, a narrower instance; in the number tower every conversion goes between concrete types below `Number`, so the value stays inside the declared type (by reading, the ways note, way 4's soundness paragraph). A ledger row, opened at batch N's gather; not a stop.
- Between N and 7b. Rung K's choice stays on today's instantiation in `bestMatchInternal`'s subtyping pass, its code unchanged, and the winner is re-instantiated by the promotion before application: the one edit to `bestMatchInternal` that K's brief reserves (`CLIMB-BATCH-N.md`, rung K, "Files it may touch") is permitted for exactly this and reported. The coercion pass keeps generics as briefed, for the calls no declaration takes unconverted (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:826`, opened and read). Re-dispatch of the converted call, `O2Z64`'s shape, cannot arise under walk before rung W lifts the load check that refuses the set today (`OverloadedFunction.java:527`; `captures/O2Z64.walk-*.txt`), so it is W's, as `option-2-soundness.md` section 4 lists.

### 4. Q1's default

**Decided: it joins the order as the tie rule for a numeral alone, stated once in the inference chapter and cited from the coercion chapter's resolution.** When a numeral's candidate types are incomparable under `⪯` (`ZZ32` against `NN32`, `CLIMB-BATCH-N.md` Q1), in the instantiation step or among converted declarations, the numeral is read as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by magnitude. It ranks nothing else. A non-numeral argument whose conversion targets are incomparable (a `ZZ32` against arms at `ZZ64` and `RR64`; an `NN32` against arms at `ZZ64` and `NN64`) stays the specification's ambiguity error, as today; no library or microGPT call reaches one, and the program writes the type. C#'s general signed-over-unsigned rule is not taken: one peer, no case. The checker's ambiguity check (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:463`, a comment with no code; opened and read) is where the default applies: rung I builds the check, applies the numeral default when the tie is a numeral's, and otherwise reports the error, the count reported.

### 5. Where it lands, and in what order

- **Batch N, run 1, as briefed, with these amendments to the record** (the fork paragraphs of rungs I and K, and rung T's chapter). Nothing of the decision lands later, so nothing is built "meanwhile".
  - **Rung I.** A generic candidate whose declared domain holds the arguments stays in the first attempt although the promotion then converts; `moreSpecificCandidate`'s coercion-first test does not count a coercion the promotion introduced; a promoted candidate is compared on its declared domain (`option-2-soundness.md` section 1, the `O2Meet` incomparability); the ambiguity check at `Functionals.scala:463` with Q1's numeral default (section 4). Tests, each on the compiled path with the compiler library: `OpAnyZW`'s pair prints `generic[ZZ64, ZZ64]`; `O2Meet` prints the meet; `O2Z64` prints `plain64` for `op(z, w)`, which closes the stock crash row (section 7); `O2Pos` prints `plain` for `gg(5, w)` and 2 for `ee(5)`; `O2Num` prints the generic at `ZZ64` for `op(1, w)`.
  - **Rung K.** Section 3's edit, permitted and reported; `OpAnyZW` under walk prints `generic[ZZ64,ZZ64]`; the split of `O2Wide` recorded, not a stop.
  - **Rung T.** The chapter states the instantiation step as the second step after the coercion chapter's resolution, in the words of section 1, with the static insertion of the instance's coercions, the dispatch on converted values, the numeral default once, and a callout that walk applies the same rule from run-time types.
- **Batch N, run 1, a small library rung** for row 484 (section 6), disjoint from I, K and T's files.
- **Batch N, run 2, rung Q**: the `exactValue` requirement (section 7), the `=` shape after the switch listed among its choices.
- **Batch 7b.** Rung S: the cross-reference sentence at `conversions-coercions.tex:472-476`, `:539-541` and `:584-591` (`option-2-soundness.md` section 1), beside its rewrite of `basic/overloading.tex:170-175` and `:292-295`. Rung W: compare on declared domains; hand the chosen generic to K's inference; dispatch the converted call again; lift the load check for the sets the checker accepts (`O2Z64`, `O2Meet`). Rung C: the expected-failure test for defect 3, as answer 9 placed it.
- **No probe first.** Probe K measured walk's rule over the 422 tests, the 62 demos and both microGPT checks: 4 calls change, none at the fork (`PROBE-K.md`, answers 3 to 6). The checker shadow measured the rule on the library and microGPT (`reviews/inference-rule-shadow.md`; `CLIMB-BATCH-N.md` section 1, "What it clears"). The decision differs from what the shadows built at one shape, reached by no recorded call (`PROBE-K.md:11`, `:17`; `before-n-questions.md` A.3). The rungs' own three-pass comparisons gate it. Way 4 would have needed the probe; way 2 does not.
- **Order.** 7C lands; N, runs 1 and 2; 7b; 8, as POSITIONS 2026-09-27's decision 5 has it. Nothing moves.

### 6. Question B, row 484

**Decided: the rule leaves it; the library fix is wanted, option 1 of `before-n-questions.md`.** Under the decision `b MAX 1` still ties: the inherited `MAX`'s `self` is the trait (`basic/overloading.tex:159-161`), which converts into nothing, so `(StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ64\], ZZ64)` and `(QQ, QQ)` are incomparable (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Coercions.java:163-190`, opened and read; `before-n-questions.md` B.2). With `ZZ64`'s own `MAX`, `(ZZ64, ZZ64)` is `⪯` both, and unique; `w MAX z`, `z MAX w` and, after rung Q, `ZZ32`'s `b MAX 1` and the library's `0 MAX (index - 1)` (`Library/SkipList.fss:310`) resolve the same way (by reading, B.2 and B.4). It is the library's device (`QQ` and `RR64`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:582-586`, `:427-429`; the compiler library on every number type, `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:198-200`; the specification's `ZZ`, `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:234-235`): 15 declarations, about 30 short lines and one test (B.5). A library rung in batch N's run 1, before Q meets the sites. Q1's default does not settle it, since no `ZZ32`-typed candidate is in the tie. Option 2 (walk reading `self` as the receiver) touches both paths and the text and leaves `QQ`'s tie; question B's option 3 is a rule beyond answer 8; leaving it costs rung Q the library's own sites.

### 7. The findings that stand under every way

- **`exactValue` and the numeral** (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:374-383`, opened and read: `else => Ratio(0, 0)`). After rung Q makes `IntLiteral` a sibling under `Number`, `x = 0` for a `ZZ32` `x` has `Number`'s `=` (`:361-371`, rung F's, `d846e3644`) and the top-level `opr =(a: Any, b: Any) = a SEQV b` (`:96`, the team's, present at `5a68404fd`) fitting unconverted; `Number`'s wins and falls to `Ratio(0, 0)`: a wrong answer, silent. By reading, `assert(v, 3, msg)`, the form of nearly every test, compares through the same path; probe Q will show the reach. So: a requirement of rung Q's brief, whichever library device it takes, each listed with the others and measured by probe Q: a numeral case in `exactValue`; `Number`'s `=` promoting to the narrowest common type, Julia's way, instead of `QQ`; or the compiled library's shape, no catch-all `=`. The correct answer now; the shape's cost (two rational conversions per `i = 0` under `exactValue`'s route) a ledger row for phase 6, since no performance decision is taken before microGPT runs compiled (POSITIONS 2026-09-19). Inside a generic body the static type is a type parameter with no coercions (`conversions-coercions.tex:363-365`), so `Number`'s `=` is reached there under every rule; the case is needed regardless.
- **The stock compiled crash**, "Overloading instanceof match failure: Should not happen!" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MiscCodegenFunctions.java:20`), on a promoted generic beside `op(ZZ64, ZZ64)` called `op(z, w)` (`captures/O2Z64.stock.txt`): a ledger row, opened by the coordinator now. Batch N's promotion removes it under the decision (`T = ZZ64`, then `plain64` at run time; measured on the rule build); rung I's `O2Z64` test closes the row.
- **The code generator's defect for two competing generic arms** (defect 3, `overloading-judgement.md` section 3.7; `O2Excl` under opt2): the decision gives it no new reach (section 2). It stays on phase 5's code-generation list, with 7b's rung C adding the gated expected-failure compiler test as answer 9 placed it. A ledger row if none exists yet; the coordinator checks.
- **The checker's missing ambiguity check** (`Functionals.scala:463`): rung I (section 4). Not a finding of the fork, but Q1's default and row 484's shape both need it, and the specification assumes it (`conversions-coercions.tex:546-549`).

## What is left open

- The split between walk and the compiled path where a static type is wider than its value (section 3): a ledger row. Way 12 (resolution per stamped instance, `conversion-overloading-ways.md` section 9) is the compiled path's own answer to the same class inside generic bodies, a phase 6 design, not this decision's.
- The `=` family's shape in the one library after the numeral switch (section 7): rung Q takes the correct device; the fast shape is a phase 6 question, with its row.
- A generic with a self-naming bound beside a catch-all: under the decision the catch-all takes mixed widths. No library or microGPT declaration has the shape; if decision D's sized signatures (phase 5) or a library extension writes one, the library's device is the meet or no catch-all, and way 4 is the way back, priced in section 1.
- A non-numeral argument whose conversion targets are incomparable (section 4): the specification's ambiguity error; no case on record.
- The promotion converts only for the selected declaration's own instantiation. A lifted type parameter fixed by the receiver (question B's `w MAX z`) is untouched by it, which is why row 484 needs its library fix.

## Files, and what was opened

- This file only. Nothing was run, built or measured.
- Opened to check a claim this judgement rests on: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1068-1095`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:440-470`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Coercions.java:150-200`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:815-860`; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:460-560`, `:580-620`; `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:240-280`, `:455-470`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi` (the `=` and `=/=` arms, `IntLiteral`); `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:24-26`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:60-75`, `:236-242`, `:2436-2450`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:90-102`, `:355-385`; `ProjectFortress/tests/CoercionOverloadRungC.fss:35-60`; `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC.fss`; `reviews/option-2-soundness/O2Tie.fss`, `O2Excl.fss`, `O2Pos.fss`, `summary.txt`; `reviews/conversion-overloading-ways/catchall-grep.txt`; `git show fc99e1ef2 --stat`; `git show d846e3644`; `git log -S` for the `Any` `=` (present at `5a68404fd`, the team's).
